Reference guide

Working with GitHub

How your website follows you from Mac to Mac: set up once, then commit, sync and check.

You will sit at a different Mac almost every session, and each Mac keeps its own separate home folder for your login. Anything you leave on one machine's Desktop stays on that machine. So your website does not live on any lab Mac: it lives on GitHub, and each Mac is just a place you work on it. You pull your site down at the start of a session, and you push your changes up before you leave. Once that habit sticks, losing work becomes almost impossible, and you get a complete history of every version of your site for free.

Never put your website folder inside OneDrive. OneDrive is fine for essays and files you upload through the browser, but it silently corrupts the hidden change-tracking data that git keeps inside your website folder. Your website folder goes on the Desktop; GitHub is its backup, not OneDrive.

This guide has four parts. You only ever do Part 1 once. Part 2 is the start-of-session routine for a machine you have not used before, and Part 3 is the rhythm of every working session. Part 4 puts your site on the live web, once, and from then on your syncs update the internet.

PART 1The first timeCreate your site and put it on GitHub. Done once, in Week 1. PART 2Sitting at a new MacGet your site back and re-introduce yourself to git. PART 3Every time you workEdit, commit, sync, and check before you leave. PART 4Going liveTurn on GitHub Pages and get a real web address. Done once.

1The first timeOnce, in Week 1

By the end of this part you will have a website folder on the Desktop, tracked by git, published to your own GitHub account, and visible at github.com. Work through the steps in order: two of them exist purely to stop errors appearing later.

Doing this in the Week 1 session? There you start from the downloaded starter project, not an empty folder. The steps are identical with two differences: wherever this guide says my-website, your folder and repository are called interaction-design, and you skip step 1.4 because the starter already has an index.html. The screenshots show the empty-folder version.

1.1Clear the clutter

The first time VS Code opens on a lab Mac it throws several things at you at once. None of them matter.

  1. Click No Thanks on the theme popup (or Keep It, it makes no difference).
  2. Close every open tab: Release Notes, Welcome, GitLens.

Ignore everything GitLens asks for. GitLens is an extension installed on the lab Macs. It will repeatedly invite you to create an account, sign in, or try Launchpad Pro. You never need any of it. The only account this module uses is your GitHub account, and the only sign-in happens in the web browser later in this guide. Also ignore the blue Sign In button at the top right of VS Code itself: that is a Microsoft account sign-in, not GitHub.

1.2Make your folder

  1. Go to File → Open Folder…
  2. In the dialog, click Desktop in the sidebar.
  3. Click New Folder, name it my-website (lower case, hyphen, no spaces), and click Create.
  4. With the new folder selected, click Open.

1.3Trust the folder

VS Code opens the folder in Restricted Mode, a safety setting for code you did not write. While the blue banner is showing, git is switched off, so this step is not optional.

  1. Click Manage in the blue banner.
  2. On the screen that opens, click the big blue Trust button.
  3. Close the Workspace Trust tab. If a file chooser opens at any point here, you have clicked Add Folder by mistake: click Cancel.

1.4Make your first page

  1. In the Explorer panel on the left, click the New File icon next to the folder name.
  2. Type index.html and press Return.
  3. Type ! then press Tab to expand the HTML boilerplate, and put a heading in the body.
  4. Save with ⌘S. The dot on the file's tab turns into an × when it is saved; a dot means unsaved changes.

1.5Tell git who you are

Every change you record is stamped with a name and an email address. The lab Macs do not know who you are, so you tell git once per machine. Skipping this is the single most common cause of a confusing error later.

  1. Go to Terminal → New Terminal. A panel opens along the bottom of the window. (If the menu is greyed out, a dialog box is open somewhere: close it and try again.)
  2. Type these two lines, pressing Return after each. Use your own name, and the email address you used for your GitHub account: 
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "yourname@example.com"

Why the email matters: GitHub links your saved changes to your account by matching this email address. Use the one you signed up to GitHub with and your commits show up as yours.

1.6Your first commit

A commit is a snapshot of your folder with a short label saying what changed. It is the basic unit of change-tracking, and you will make many of them every session.

  1. Click the Source Control icon in the left bar (third one down, the branching lines).
  2. Click Initialize Repository. This is a once-per-website action: it switches git on for this folder.
  3. Your file appears under Changes with a U (untracked, meaning new). Type a short message in the box, something like My first commit, and click Commit.
  4. A box asks whether to stage all changes and commit them directly. Click Yes. (Staging is choosing which changes go in the snapshot; "all of them" is right for this module.)

If you see "Make sure you configure your user.name and user.email in git", you skipped step 1.5. None of the buttons on this dialog help: click Cancel, do step 1.5, then click Commit again.

1.7Publish to GitHub

So far the snapshot only exists on this Mac. Publishing creates a copy of your website on GitHub, under your account, and connects the two. This is the longest step because GitHub needs to check who you are, which happens in the web browser.

  1. After your first commit, the button changes to Publish Branch. Click it.
  2. A dialog says the GitHub extension wants to sign in. Click Allow. Your web browser opens on github.com.
  3. Sign in with your GitHub username and password, then complete two-factor authentication with your phone.
  4. On the Authorize Visual Studio Code page, check it says your username, then click Continue or the green authorise button.
  5. When the browser says you have successfully signed in, go back to VS Code.

Back in VS Code, a box drops down from the top asking where to publish.

The top option is a private repository, and it is selected by default. Do not press Return. Click the second option, Publish to GitHub public repository. Your site needs to be public to go on the web later, and everything in this folder is coursework, not secrets.

1.8See it on github.com

Click Open on GitHub in the notification, or go to github.com and open your profile. Your repository is there, with your file and your commit message next to it. This page is your proof that the work is safely off the lab Mac, and you will check it at the end of every session from now on.

2Sitting at a new MacStart of a session

Next session you will probably be at a different machine, and your Desktop folder from last week is not on it. That is by design: your site lives on GitHub, so you clone it, which means downloading a full working copy, history and all. There are only two steps, plus one about what to ignore.

2.1Clone your website

  1. Open VS Code and clear any clutter (step 1.1).
  2. On the Welcome tab click Clone Git Repository… (or the Clone Repository button in the Explorer panel, they do the same thing).
  3. In the box that drops down from the top, click Clone from GitHub.
  4. If the browser opens asking you to sign in to GitHub, work through it exactly as in step 1.7, then come back.
  5. Pick yourusername/my-website from the list of your repositories.
  6. In the folder chooser, select Desktop and click Select as Repository Destination.
  7. When asked, click Open.

2.2Tell git who you are, again

Your name and email from step 1.5 were saved on last week's machine, not this one. Run the same two lines in a new terminal (Terminal → New Terminal): 

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "yourname@example.com"

Do it now, before you start working, and the confusing dialog from step 1.6 never appears.

2.3Things to ignore on a fresh machine

  • GitLens will fill the sidebar with Create Free Account, Sign In and Launchpad Pro. None of it is needed; close it and carry on.
  • The Recent list on the Welcome tab remembers folders from whoever used the machine's login state last, or from machines you are no longer at. Always clone; never trust Recent.
  • The blue Sign In button top right is a Microsoft account. Not needed.

3Every time you workThe session rhythm

This is the habit the whole guide exists for. You edit, you commit whenever you finish a meaningful chunk, and you sync before you leave. Commit little and often: a commit that says Added the hero image is far more useful to you later than one that says everything from today.

3.1Edit and save

Work on your site as normal. As soon as you save a change, Source Control notices: the file appears under Changes with an M (modified), and a number appears on the Source Control icon.

3.2Commit

Type a short message describing what you changed, click Commit, and click Yes if the staging box appears.

3.3Sync

Committing records the snapshot on this Mac only. The button now reads Sync Changes with an arrow and a number: that is how many commits exist only on this machine. Click it, and they are pushed up to GitHub.

3.4Check before you leave

Open your repository on github.com and refresh. Your latest commit message should be showing at the top. If it is, your work is off this machine and next week's clone will include it. If it is not, you have committed but not synced: go back to VS Code and click Sync Changes. Once your site is live (Part 4), your public web page also updates itself a minute or two after every sync.

End of session, every session

  1. Save everything: ⌘S in every tab with a dot.
  2. Commit anything left under Changes, with a message.
  3. Click Sync Changes until the button goes quiet.
  4. Refresh your repository on github.com and see your last commit message.
  5. Sign out of github.com in the browser before you log off the Mac.

4Going liveOnce per website

Everything so far keeps your work safe. This part makes it public: GitHub Pages takes what is on your repository's main branch and serves it as a real website with its own address. You switch it on once, and from then on every commit you sync goes live on the internet a minute or two later, automatically. Nothing about your weekly routine changes.

Live means live. Everything in your repository is already publicly visible, and Pages puts it on a friendly web address anyone can visit. Coursework belongs here; passwords, private photos and anything you would not hand a stranger do not.

4.1Find the Pages settings

  1. On your repository page at github.com, click Settings at the right-hand end of the tab row.
  2. In the left sidebar, click Pages.

4.2Deploy from main

  1. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch.
  2. Under Branch, choose main and leave the folder as / (root).
  3. Click Save.

4.3Get your address

The build takes a minute or two. Refresh the Pages settings page until a box appears at the top saying Your site is live at… followed by your address. The shape is always the same: https://yourusername.github.io/my-website/. That works because your home page is called index.html, the one filename the web serves by default.

From now on, publishing is automatic. Commit and sync as in Part 3, wait a minute or two, refresh your live address, and the change is on the web. There is nothing extra to click, ever.

?When it goes wrong

  • "Make sure you configure your user.name and user.email" when committing: you are on a machine that does not know you yet. Cancel, run the two lines from step 2.2, commit again.
  • A menu is greyed out: a dialog box is open somewhere, possibly hidden behind the window. Find it, close it, try again.
  • You published as private by accident: on github.com go to your repository's Settings, scroll to the Danger Zone, and choose Change visibility → public. Or ask a tutor.
  • Commit button says Sync Changes but you have edits: your edits are not saved or not committed yet. Save, commit, then sync.
  • The browser sign-in page never comes back to VS Code: close the browser tab, click Publish Branch (or retry the clone) and go through the sign-in again.
  • The live site is not showing your latest change: give it two minutes, then refresh with ⇧⌘R to skip the browser's saved copy. Still old? Check github.com shows the change; if it does not, you have not synced.
